transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Patel, thank you for coming in to see me today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I’m here. I’ve got my notebook. You said on the phone this was urgent.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is. I want to start by saying that this is a very difficult conversation to have, and I recognize how stressful it is to be called back into the clinic like this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I’m already stressed. I’ve spent the last forty-eight hours processing a cancer diagnosis. I’ve been reading every single word of the pathology report you sent me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you have. And that is why I need to talk to you. There has been some confusion regarding the lab results.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Confusion? What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Things didn't go quite right with the processing of your biopsy. We’ve discovered an issue with how the specimen was handled in the lab.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't follow. What "issue"? Did the test fail?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are looking into some discrepancies. It seems there was a problem with the labeling process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I’m sorry, you’re being incredibly vague. Are you telling me the diagnosis is wrong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are still investigating the exact sequence of events, but we believe the results you received may not be yours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are telling me that for two days I have believed I have cancer because of a "problem with labeling"?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am very sorry. Our team failed you here, and we take full responsibility for this mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is exactly why I don't trust this place. I told you when I signed the intake forms that I needed total transparency. Now you're telling me you can't even keep track of whose tissue is whose?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is completely understandable that you feel betrayed right now. To have your world turned upside down for two days and then find out it was because of a clinical error is an agonizing experience.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Agonizing? I’ve been calling my parents. I’ve been looking at oncology clinics. I’ve spent forty-eight hours in a nightmare.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can only imagine how exhausting and isolating those last two days have been for you, especially while you were trying to plan for a future you thought was suddenly precarious.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what happens now? Do I actually have cancer or not?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is what we are working to resolve right now. Because the labeling was compromised, we cannot rely on that specific report.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Then why aren't you just telling me the answer?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Because we don't have a confirmed answer yet. We are currently auditing the lab logs to see where the switch occurred.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is unbelievable. You’re basically saying you lost my sample?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I don't have the confirmation on that yet. We are checking if your sample was given to another patient or if it is still in the lab under a different name.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And the other person? The person who got my results? Or the person I thought I was?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are in the process of identifying and contacting the other patient involved.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel like I'm in a glitch. I'm a software engineer, I deal with errors all day, but usually, the error isn't "you have a malignant tumor."

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a terrifying position to be in, feeling like the ground has shifted beneath you twice in forty-eight hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want to see the logs. I want to see the investigation.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. You want to see the actual evidence of how this happened so you don't have to rely on my word.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes. Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here is the plan. I am going to call the head of pathology right now to find out if your original tissue is recovered. I will call you by 5:00 PM today to tell you if we have found your sample.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And if you haven't?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: If we haven't found it by 5:00 PM, I will call you anyway to tell you that. Then, tomorrow morning, we will schedule a repeat biopsy to get you a definitive answer.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I’m not sure I want to let you people touch me again.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a completely fair reaction. If you decide you want a second opinion or want the repeat biopsy done at a different facility, I will personally handle the transfer of your records to make it happen.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I need to think about that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Please take all the time you need. I will be the one calling you at 5:00 PM.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts the patient, remains regulated despite significant pushback, and allows the patient to express their distress fully.

E.justification: The resident uses platitudes like 'some confusion' and 'things didn't go quite right' and does not explicitly name the error (labeling switch) until the patient prompts them, and no comprehension checks are performed.

A.justification: The resident uses direct apology language ('I am very sorry'), explicitly states 'Our team failed you here,' and takes full responsibility without deflection.

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions ('betrayed', 'agonizing', 'terrifying') and references the patient's specific experience of planning for a precarious future.

T.justification: The resident provides specific next steps with a clear timeline (call by 5:00 PM today, repeat biopsy tomorrow) and a patient role (deciding on a second opinion), but does not address prevention.
